newsitem.title: UK: UK's Cook to spell out new British foreign policy.
newsitem.headline: UK's Cook to spell out new British foreign policy.

text.p: New Foreign Secretary Robin Cook will on Monday publicly spell out for the first time his vision of Britain's foreign policy after 18 years of Conservative rule often marred by disputes with international partners.
Cook is due to give his first formal news conference at 11.45 a.m. (1045 GMT) and will also release a mission statement outlining what he wants the Foreign Office to achieve.
"I think it will be in plain English. He wants to motivate and enthuse," said one official.
The new Labour government says it will end the increasingly antagonistic relations with the European Union and other nations which marred the end of Conservative rule.

The other members of the 15-nation bloc could only watch as the Conservative party split in two over Europe, with the vocal so-called "Eurosceptic" wing opposed to further integration with the EU often dominating the headlines.

Cook and his colleagues have already started trying to smooth ruffled relations with the EU and have made it clear that human rights will play a much greater role in the formulation of Britain's foreign policy.

"Nothing succeeds like political success on changing the nature of negotiations. Domestic strength does mean foreign policy strength," said one official, referring to the massive majority which Labour enjoys.

The little red-bearded Scotsman belongs to the traditional left wing of Labour. He still stays true to internationalist roots of old Labour, which eschewed militarism and the arms trade, and says he wants to boost the role of the British Commonwealth.

There is little doubt that Cook's blunt no-nonsense style and the change of government has, temporarily at least, cracked the stiff facade at the Foreign Office, renowned for turning out cool, calm and above all else dignified diplomats.

"I've met some very senior people who are almost beside themselves with glee. It's like looking at little boys let loose in a confectionery store," said one diplomat who has visited the foreign office since Labour won.

"I'm sure most of the senior foreign office people quietly voted for the Conservatives but none of them were ever Eurosceptics. These last few years can't have been easy for them," the diplomat added. Officials, at pains not to tarnish the achievements and working style of outgoing foreign secretary Malcolm Rifkind, say it has been a pleasure dealing with Cook so far.

"People have enjoyed the last few days because they have had the opportunity to speak to the minister about policy matters. People have enjoyed contributing to issues," said one, even finding time to crack a joke about Cook's love of horse-racing.
"(Racing newspaper) Sporting Life is being read up carefully in the office," the official said.
"And it would be good to think that some of our more boring meetings could be held at Kempton Park (racecourse)."
